question: Can a curriculum build one skill on top of another? Three tests: stacking, combination, order.
measure: How far the jaws follow a cube moved 20 mm mid-episode (follow gain, 0 to 1), and how many pickups survive a soft elbow.
outcome: Stack: yes. Combine: yes. Order: no effect. Read it as "skills add up, but these two do not depend on each other".
setup: A policy is the network that drives the arm. Earlier we showed that one change to the training data gives the policy one skill. A teacher that corrects its own mistakes teaches it to follow the cube when it moves ("look"). Randomized servo physics teaches it to cope when the elbow goes soft ("motor"). A curriculum needs such skills to build on each other.

parts.title: Do the two skills stack in one policy?
parts.why: If training on both changes gave neither skill, the changes interfere and no curriculum can work.
parts.did: Trained one policy on half of each kind of data, then moved the cube 20 mm mid-episode, and separately made the elbow soft.

predictions.text: It keeps at least 80% of pickups with a soft elbow

parts.conclusion: No interference. Both skills are there; the motor one is slightly diluted (72% and 79% against the 80% bar), and twice the data did not fix that.

parts.title: Do they combine in one episode?
parts.why: No training episode contains both changes at once, so this tests whether skills compose or were only learned separately.
parts.did: A new probe moves the cube and softens the elbow in the same episode.

predictions.text: The baseline, look-only and every CNN do not

parts.conclusion: Replanning every 30 steps, the skills combine like independent parts (0.77 kept against 0.73). Replanning every 90 steps, nothing handles both.

parts.title: Does having one skill make the next cheaper?
parts.why: This is the curriculum question. If yes, the order you teach skills in saves data.
parts.did: Started from a policy with and without the other skill and trained 5,000 more steps on 300, 1,200 and 4,800 placements.

predictions.text: Adding motor: the start that already has look leads by 0.10
Adding look: the start that already has motor leads by 0.10

parts.conclusion: No order effect: the lead was −0.00 and +0.02 against the 0.10 bar. Each skill is learned from 300 placements from any start.

trust.text: Same 100 placements and the same shift plans for every policy
The half-and-half policy has the same 7,200-placement budget as the three single policies
Both starts in the order test had the same training: 40,000 steps on 7,200 placements
The motor data and the look data were captured on different scenes
One training seed for parts 1 and 2. Two skills only. Simulation only.

Its premise, one data change gives one skill, holds for the aimed pair only. Experiment 52's full matrix (read 2026-11-25) shows skills nobody aimed at: every policy follows a moved square (gain +0.51 to +0.96 on the nominal scene, teacher 0.00), and the motor data alone brings shift-following when replanning every 30 steps.
The next step proposed here, a skill built on an earlier one such as set-down on a moved square, is weaker than it reads: every policy already sets down on a moved square.
This experiment's combination stage rewrote experiment 52's nominal-scene result files with three probes only, which is why 18 of 52's predictions went unread until 2026-11-25.

meaning: Stacking and combining are supported. Order is not, but this pair was a weak test: neither skill needs the other.
lesson: The two "failed" marks only mean something because the bar was written down before the run.

next.title: A skill built on an earlier one: retry after a failed grasp
next.why: Needs "look" first. This is a real test of order.

next.title: Why is the motor skill diluted in mixed policies?
next.why: Twice the data did not fix it (73% / 63%).
